articles.title: US Army acquisition command awards contracts worth $6.8B in 2026
articles.snippet: The Mission and Installation Contracting Command awarded 21,450 contracts in fiscal 2026 valued at $6.8 billion in total, a boost from the year prior.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Army’s contracting and acquisition support command finished fiscal 2026 with a $1 billion increase from the prior year’s contracting obligations.
The Mission and Installation Contracting Command awarded 21,450 contracts in fiscal 2026 valued at $6.8 billion, with $2.9 billion going to American small businesses, according to a Friday release.
As the command moves to expand its role in the service’s modernization and innovation acquisition, it increased its contracting by more than $1 billion from fiscal 2025, which had 22,000 contract actions valued at $5.5 billion.
Growing facility modernization requirements, increased acquisition authorities and adding the 410th Contracting Support Brigade to the MICC drove the increase from last fiscal year, the release says.
“Some growth was expected as we welcomed the 410th Contracting Support Brigade into the command,” MICC Command Sgt. Maj. JennyAnne Bright said in an early October message to the team. “But $1 billion in growth reflects the growing demand for your expertise and your ability to deliver contracting solutions to Soldiers and our mission partners at the point of need.”
The command had more than 299,000 Government Purchase Card transitions with a value of more than $520 million, giving extra “purchasing power” in support of soldiers, installations and mission partners across the service, the release states.
The MICC employed a wider range of acquisition authorities to address more complex regional requirements and to expand industry collaboration, such as Other Transactions Authorities, Small Business Innovation Research Phase III and Multiple Award Task Orders.
The command’s Facilities, Operations, Readiness, Growth and Experience, or FORGE, initiatives consolidated multiple modernization requirements into larger efforts that grouped related requirements to increase effectiveness, the release says.
One of the MICC FORGE initiatives gave a $169.1 million Other Transaction agreement in support of 17 modernization projects, while another established around $987 million in modernization efforts.
Alongside modernization efforts, for the 12th consecutive year, MICC exceeded its assigned small business goals despite a workforce decrease.
“Exceeding our small business goals across the board for a 12th consecutive year is a phenomenal achievement by our contracting and small business professionals,” Luis Trinidad, director of the Army Contracting Command-MICC Office of Small Business Programs, said in the release. “Operating with a 30% reduction in personnel, our team rose to meet a more demanding workload.”
The command’s small business-eligible dollars increased by $104.8 million, requiring more detailed reviews of acquisition packages.
For fiscal 2027, which began Oct. 1, MICC expects a continued boost in modernization requirements and demand for enterprise contracting solutions, forcing innovative acquisition authorities that are tailored to specific mission and soldier needs, according to the release.
Because MICC was established in October 2008, the end of fiscal 2026 aligned with the command’s 18th anniversary. It was founded under the Army Contracting Command as the Installation Contracting Command, and then redesignated as MICC shortly after.
“In just two short decades, MICC has grown into an indispensable element of the Army’s mission, and that legacy is entirely due to the hard work and excellence of professionals like you,” MICC Commanding General Brig. Gen. Freddy L. Adams said in the release.
Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

articles.title: Australia gets the ball rolling on medium-range air defense
articles.snippet: Recognizing the massive gap, Canberra has launched a formal tender for a medium-range, ground-based air defense solution for the Australian Army.
articles.full_text:
PERTH, Australia — To protect a whole continent, Australia has only a regiment’s worth of NASAMS short-range air defense systems. Recognizing this is not nearly enough, Canberra has launched a formal tender for a medium-range, ground-based air defense solution for the Australian Army.
The Department of Defence launched an industry solicitation for the project, christened Project Land 6504, on Oct. 13. The potential deal has already attracted interest globally, with vendors from Europe, Israel, South Korea, Turkey and the United States eying the requirement Down Under.
A primary motivation for filling the gaping hole in Australian defenses is China’s rising military prowess. Alarming many, the People’s Liberation Army sent a naval task group to circumnavigate Australia in early 2025, and then China fired an intercontinental ballistic missile into the South Pacific in July this year.
With China possessing the world’s most diverse missile arsenal, Australia knows it needs better defenses. Land 6504 is therefore looking for a defensive system capable of shooting down ballistic missiles in their terminal phase of flight, as well as address subsonic air-breathing threats.
The National Defence Strategy 2026 prioritized missile defense, calling for “accelerated introduction of medium-range, ground-based, active missile defense through investment in missile launchers and munitions and integrating them with the Australian Defence Force’s command-and-control systems.”
This envisioned off-the-shelf system is expected to be a “proven capability,” contributing to a national, integrated system, the solicitation reads.
Money is a perennial problem, however, as AUKUS nuclear-powered submarines soak up available defense funds.
But perhaps the greatest risk is the lightning speed at which this Australian project is moving. Final selection of the vendor is to occur by the end of 2027. The solution is to perform live-firing in Exercise Talisman Saber in mid-2029, and an initial operational capability achieved in the early 2030s.
Importantly, the expeditionary air-defense system must integrate with radars from CEA Technologies and the Joint Air Battle Management System being developed by Lockheed Martin Australia.
Because of the time constraints, Canberra is pursuing direct commercial sale and U.S. Foreign Military Sales (FMS) avenues simultaneously.
The timing of the tender may boost the chances of non-American missile suppliers, as the U.S. grapples with depleted magazines after expending large amounts of missiles in its conflict with Iran.
A recent Congressional Research Service report warned, “Finite U.S. industrial base capacity introduces trade-offs between filling FMS orders and replenishing U.S. stockpiles. FMS delivery delays may result in cancellations, potentially affecting U.S. and partner interoperability and integration.”
Other options are available, however. For example, Australia could add AMRAAM-ER extended-range missiles to its existing NASAMS.
John Fry, managing director of Kongsberg Australia, told Defense News: “We’re definitely interested in that program. I think the great thing with the NASAMS architecture is Kongsberg and Raytheon are evolving that into full-spectrum air defense.”
Elsewhere, Lockheed Martin Australia fired an SM-2 missile from a trailer launcher in June, utilizing the Aegis combat system and a CEA radar. This demonstrated how a hybrid air defense system can make use of components already available in Australia.
Gordon Arthur is an Asia correspondent for Defense News. After a 20-year stint working in Hong Kong, he now resides in New Zealand. He has attended military exercises and defense exhibitions in about 20 countries around the Asia-Pacific region.

articles.title: US Army showing interest in G/ATOR missile-killing radar, Northrop says
articles.snippet: Northrop Grumman’s new multi-mission radar system has earned high marks from Marine Corps leadership. The U.S. Army has taken notice.
articles.full_text:
Northrop Grumman’s new multi-mission radar system has earned effusive praise from Marine Corps leaders as it surges well past the halfway point in fielding. On the heels of that success, officials said this month, other potential customers, including the U.S. Army, have expressed interest in the system.
The AN/TPS-80 Ground/Air Task Oriented Radar, or G/ATOR, is the Marine Corps’ solution for defending against a broad range of airborne threats, particularly in the Pacific littorals.
It replaces five older radar systems, and last year received an extended-range software upgrade that boosted its capability and advanced its ability to differentiate friends or foes in the air.
In a call with reporters Oct. 7, Northrop Director of Mission Systems Paul Weaver said the company had delivered 43 of the 60 G/ATOR systems the Marine Corps has ordered, of which five are designated for the Air Force and one for Navy test and evaluation.
“Demand for the system in theater right now is high, and it’s based on that performance,” Weaver said. “We’ve been making modifications to the system based on customer input for the last four or five years. We’ve made some hardware modifications that extended its range, and we’re constantly making software improvements to adapt to the specific threat environment, whether that be [unmanned aerial systems], from the smallest to the largest, and other potential threats that they face.”
Weaver said the company was “actively engaged at the headquarters level” with the Marine Corps and the Air Force about how best to employ G/ATOR and had recently begun engagements with the Army as well. While he deferred on saying whether the Army had interest in acquiring the radar system, he said its capabilities had broad appeal across the services.
“When you put a number of these systems in the field, operating in a complementary way, you can stay in constant movement and complicate the adversary’s target cycle,” Weaver said. “That is of interest to every service that’s currently in conflict right now. So, to the level that we’re engaged with the Army and the Air Force, it all comes back to its current performance and the agility that this advanced platform potentially offers.”
At 9,000 pounds, G/ATOR is small and light enough to be transported by C-130 Hercules or MV-22 Osprey aircraft. It can be set up and emplaced by a four-person crew in under ten minutes, and can flex in power settings from 60 kilowatts for medium-range targets to 75 kilowatts for longer-range kills. Initial fielding to the Marine Corps began in 2018, and service leaders have suggested more recently that they might soon expand their acquisition plan.
“We learned that it’s much more capable than we thought,” Brig. Gen. Christopher Haar, now commander of the 3rd Marine Logistics Group, told Military Times last December. “And now there’s a demand for us to get that in more units, and to potentially increase the number of those systems that we buy.”
The War Zone reported last month that the Corps’ Pacific-based 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit had employed the service’s Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations (EABO) concept for the first time in combat during operations in support of the Operation Epic Fury conflict with Iran. It’s not clear if the G/ATOR system was part of that concept employment. But Weaver did suggest that the current conflict is highlighting its strengths.
With its lightweight footprint and capable 360-degree active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, the system, he said, can be flown into an austere location to establish an expeditionary air base, allowing the establishment of a surveillance perimeter while also enabling airspace control. According to the company, the system can identify launch points of hostile fires ranging from mortars to artillery and serve as a ground-based air traffic control manager. Drone warfare, Weaver said, brings out other strengths.
“It’s proving in recent conflicts and around the globe to perform exceptionally well in clutter, which makes it very helpful in identifying all classes of UASs and cruise missiles,” he said. “It’s not only providing awareness of what’s in the airspace around it at all altitudes. It provides weapons quality data and that performance, which means the warfighter can not only see it but also connect it to any available countermeasure that it has, whether that be kinetic or non-kinetic, and address it appropriately.”

articles.title: A shifting landscape: Where the US Army moved in 2026 and what may be on the horizon
articles.snippet: As seasons signal the waning months of 2026, the U.S. Army’s operational map continues to evolve.
articles.full_text:
As seasons signal the waning months of 2026, the U.S. Army’s operational map continues to evolve.
New commands and force restructuring have put greater emphasis on the Western Hemisphere and Indo-Pacific, while the ongoing conflict with Iran and Ukraine’s fight against Russia have complicated the force posture in U.S. Central Command’s area of operations and what might have been a troop drawdown in Europe, respectively.
Taken together, the moves offer a snapshot of locations the Army prioritized in 2026, and where it might turn its focus next.
Western Hemisphere
In a sweeping force restructure, the Army stood up a new Western Hemisphere Command in late 2025, consolidating three major commands under a single headquarters at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. The move aligns with the 2026 National Defense Strategy, which prioritized defending the “U.S. Homeland” and the Western Hemisphere over the U.S.’s persistent goal of opposing China.
The service shuttered some of its global advisory brigades, retaining only two Security Force Assistance Brigades, or SFABs. One of the remaining SFABs is regionally aligned to U.S. Southern Command, and the Army reported that the Western Hemisphere Command would assume responsibilities previously shouldered by the Security Force Assistance Command.
U.S. Southern Command also activated Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere in August, creating a standing headquarters to coordinate regional operations with 18 partner nations and target cartels and other transnational criminal networks.
The Army also, in partnership with Panama, revived its jungle school course in the Central American country after a decades-long hiatus. Officials have said that maintaining jungle warfare skills is applicable in the Indo-Pacific region as well.
Central Command
Force posture in the Central Command area of operations — spanning the Middle East, Central and South Asia, and Northeast Africa — continues to change. In mid-April, U.S. troops shut down several American bases in Syria, handing them over to government forces and ending a 10-year presence in the country.
Last month, the U.S. formally left Iraq after more than two decades of war, spurring warnings from security experts who say the withdrawal could give Iran, its allies and the Islamic State increased freedom to operate in the country.
However, amid the U.S.’s war with Iran, the U.S. has extended an 82nd Airborne Division deployment to the region, keeping troops for a total of one year. In February, the Army announced that a brigade from the 10th Mountain Division was set to deploy to the region as well, though it did not provide a specific timeline.
Speaking broadly about the force — not just the Army — a senior U.S. official told Reuters in June that the U.S. planned to maintain its robust military presence in the region as hostilities between the U.S. and Iran persist.
Europe
In the European theater, the U.S. Army’s force posture appears to be in flux.
Shortly after the Army abruptly scrapped the planned deployment of the 2nd Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Cavalry Division, to Poland, the Pentagon announced in May it was deploying 5,000 troops to the country.
Defense Department spokesperson Sean Parnell called the surge a “temporary delay” of the Trump administration’s plan to reduce the number of Brigade Combat Teams assigned to Europe from four to three.
This summer, the Pentagon launched a broad review of U.S. troops, bases and force posture across Europe. The review, which is expected to take up to six months, comes after the Trump administration’s calls for European countries to take on heftier NATO defense responsibilities.
Still, the Army continues to participate in multinational training exercises in Europe, like Dynamic Front 2026 and Exercise Saber Junction.
Europe’s theater has been particularly rife with lessons about drone warfare. Maj. Gen. Christopher Norrie, the acting Commanding General of U.S. Army Europe and Africa, said in a September briefing that troops rotated through the Army’s “training support mission” in Ukraine’s capital to learn about drone units.
Indo-Pacific
Deterrence appeared to define the Indo-Pacific theater in 2026.
“In the big scheme of things, our highest duty is to deter,” Gen. Ronald Clark, commander of U.S. Army Pacific, told Military Times in an interview.
Earlier in the year, Exercise Balikatan 2026 — the largest drill of the series yet — was held in the Philippines and included troops from the Philippines, the U.S., Australia, Canada, France, Japan and New Zealand. The exercise’s focus, Clark said, had shifted over the years from counterterrorism to “large-scale combat operations.”
Though Chinese leader Xi Jinping ordered troops to seize Taiwan by 2027, the outlying island is conspicuously absent from the 2026 National Defense Strategy.
In June, the Army launched a new Indo-Pacific multi-domain command that brought together conventional forces and the Cross Domain Contact Layer, a continuous network that combines sensors, drones, precision weapons, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare and more.
According to a May 2025 executive order, the Army plans to create four such commands, including one Multi-Domain Command—Japan.
Africa
The Army has reduced some of its Africa-focused force structure, shuttering the 2nd Security Force Assistance Brigade, previously aligned with U.S. Africa Command, late last year.
The command has seen a 75% force drawdown in the last ten years, creating what Gen. Dagvin Anderson, the command’s top leader, described in testimony before Congress as “an intelligence black hole,” and said the organization was operating with “minimum necessary resources.”
The U.S. special operations task force in Somalia posted an ad for three cultural and political advisors in late May.
The Arctic
The Marine Corps announced this year that it is moving troops deeper into Alaska with an initiative — aptly called “Campaign - Alaska” — designed to build a more persistent presence in the Arctic and prepare service members for extreme cold-weather operations.
The new rotating force will train and experiment in the frigid conditions and will likely add to interservice operations and exercises with partners like the Army’s Alaska-based 11th Airborne Division.
While the Army announced no major force posture changes in Alaska or the Arctic, the Army Corps of Engineers is working to expand where troops can operate in the region.
Researchers are developing new standards for landing Black Hawks and Chinooks on frozen lakes after testing found that aircraft could land on thinner ice than previous Army doctrine allowed, possibly opening up 25% more terrain for aviation operations.
Eve Sampson is a reporter and former Army officer. She has covered conflict across the world, writing for The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Associated Press.

articles.title: Ukrainian defense firms get creative to try and break through export restrictions
articles.snippet: Speaking to Breaking Defense in Washington and Lviv, companies made clear that reform efforts to allow weapons exports have not gone far enough.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Ukraine recorded its largest presence ever at AUSA this year, with 14 companies attending as part of the stand-alone Ukrainian defense pavilion. This marked the country’s first return to the show since 2017, before Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
But despite the presence of these firms at America’s largest defense conference, a longstanding challenge remains: exporting weapon systems from Ukraine is inherently complicated.
“For Ukrainian defense companies, bringing our innovations to international markets is a pretty complex regulatory environment,” Yurii Hundych, chief commercial officer at Meta Bureau, told Breaking Defense on the sidelines of the show.
In April, in a long-awaited move, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that the war-torn country would change its current export regime, which since 2022 has prohibited the transfer of military goods to other countries, to partially allow the sale of some domestically produced weapons to allies deemed non-cooperative with Russia.
At the time, the head of state stated in an X post that Ukrainian companies would receive “a real opportunity to enter partner countries’ markets,” provided that the country’s armed forces were entitled to obtain the required amount of weapons first and “only what companies can produce beyond state orders will be exported.”
However, six months later, Ukrainian firms tell Breaking Defense that a simple path forward has yet to materialize.
“There is a significant gap between the formal procedure and its practical implementation,” a spokesperson for Phantom Defense, who wished to remain anonymous for security reasons, told Breaking Defense in Lviv last month. “The industry is still gaining practical experience with the new export licensing process, and companies are exploring ways to navigate it. … But the licensing procedure can be a bottleneck for companies looking to start exporting.”
Instead, companies are left to pursue a variety of bureaucratic options, with no clear understanding of what will work or what won’t at any given time.
“While obtaining a traditional export license is a challenging process, we are exploring new innovative opportunities for international cooperation,” Hundych said during AUSA.
The Export Options
So how are companies trying to get around these obstacles? Industry officials say there are a number of ways.
Denys Nikolayenko, CEO and co-founder of Oko Camera, a Ukrainian manufacturer of thermal and infrared cameras for drones and unmanned ground vehicles on the frontline, highlighted that the rules are different for dual-source companies such as his. He explained that since the company is registered and classified as a dual-use company, it has been exporting to European and non-European customers with much greater ease than his contemporaries, who are pure defense companies.
“For other defense companies, the [export] license process has been more complex to navigate and is essentially stuck. In fact, there is currently no working export [procedure] for Ukrainian defense tech: draft laws that will form policies on this matter are still pending,” Nikolayenko told Breaking Defense. “As a result, some Ukrainian producers are either not operating at full-capacity or reducing their production volumes, as government contracts currently do not cover all production of Ukrainian companies.”
Of course, pure military firms can’t simply claim to be dual-use and get around current restrictions, which leaves them looking for other solutions, including trying to get selected for defense efforts abroad.
For Meta Bureau, which claims over 30 Ukrainian brigades use its AI-powered drones, that includes participating in the US Department of Defense’s Drone Dominance program. “We see DDP as a promising way to build partnerships and expand our international presence,” Hundych said. (Hundych didn’t explain further how joining DDP would change exportability, but Kyiv, always eager to deepen ties with Washington, would likely allow Ukrainian drones selected by the Pentagon to move abroad.)
Another model that Ukrainian manufacturers have at their disposal are international partnership agreements signed with other allies.
Ukrainian firms have sought to sign cooperation agreements with foreign companies. Phantom Defense appears to be one such company, being present this week for the first time at the AUSA conference in Washington, promoting some of its counter-drone and electronic warfare systems abroad.
But, the spokesperson said, few of these agreements have actually resulted in sales: “According to analytical studies, there are more than 180 international partnerships in the Ukrainian defense industry, but more than 20 [percent] are still at the MoU stage and have not yet moved into practical implementation,” he said.
Other avenues for international cooperation that companies can consider, he added, include localizing production, where foreign government funding supports collaboration between a Ukrainian producer and an industrial partner outside Ukraine, and the “Danish model,” where another country funds Ukrainian firms to produce weapons which are then used both by Ukraine and sold back to the partner country.
“The Danish model — direct procurement of Ukrainian systems financed by foreign governments — based on publicly available information, this one has provided a practical mechanism for authorities abroad to procure Ukrainian defense systems,” the Phantom representative said.
Unfortunately for these companies and others, an easy path forward doesn’t appear to be coming anytime soon.
According to Impact Law, a Ukrainian law firm, on July 8, the country’s Cabinet of Ministers formally adopted Resolution No. 875, dubbed “Certain Matters of International Transfer of Goods for the Duration of Martial Law in Ukraine,” covering both military and dual-use goods. Specifically, the resolution addressed the Drone Deal format, a separate, long-term partnership between Ukraine and allies focused on joint production or supply agreements in the field of unmanned systems.
In a report, the law firm explained that this new resolution “does not repeal the general export control procedures for military and dual-use goods” and that, to qualify for these exports, the State Service for Export Control must issue a license. The manufacturer must submit an application, along with other supporting documents, and the review period may not exceed 30 calendar days.

articles.title: Army feels ‘growing pains’ as it integrates Anduril NGC2 tech with older comms
articles.snippet: “It wasn’t seamless, and we learned a lot,” Brig. Gen. Shane Taylor told Breaking Defense.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — When the Army for the first time attempted to integrate Next Generation Command and Control (NGC2) tech from defense firm Anduril into its existing comms systems, not everything went exactly to plan, Army and company officials revealed to Breaking Defense this week.
“It wasn’t seamless, and we and we learned a lot,” Brig. Gen. Shane Taylor, Portfolio Management Executive for Command and Control Information Network (C2IN), said on the sidelines of the annual AUSA conference this week. “There’s always growing point pains in these. I just think that a lot of the things that we saw out there were normal, like all right, we’re putting … a group that hasn’t necessarily worked together, so it’s just that normal growing pains with that.”
The test had come in September, when the Army’s 25th Infantry Division attempted to use Anduril’s Lattice platform during Lightning Surge 5 in Hawaii, which the Army described as a “multi-phase campaign to modernize its command-and-control architecture.” Up until then, Anduril’s NGC2 tech had been used by the 4th ID in Colorado where it was paired with new, mostly commercial hardware and software.
Lockheed Martin, which is leading the integration on the 25th ID’s portion of the NGC2 architecture, served as the integrator for Anduril’s platform. Chandra Marshall, vice president of multi-domain combat solutions at the defense giant, told Breaking Defense the company expected “it would be a challenge.”
“I would say outside of Lockheed Martin, yes, I think some people are surprised at how much of a challenge it has been,” Marshall said in an interview at the AUSA conference.
She explained scaling with Lattice was an issue passing data through the system “just is not at the state it should be right now with bringing in the Lattice product.”
An Anduril official, for his part, acknowledged the growing pains, but noted that they discovered technical limitations with the communications architecture writ large.
“It was our first time with a host of technologies at the 25th [ID],” James Craven, Program Manager for NGC2 for Anduril, said in an interview Wednesday. “Working on TSM radios that were not the same waveform or configuration that we had used at 4th ID, and [Lightning Surge] was also several novel mission threads as well.”
Getting Lattice and the older comms structure on the same page will be key to the Army’s NGC2 efforts, as Army and industry officials noted that the 25th ID’s architecture is largely representative of what they’ll have to build on top of as they begin to baseline and field other units within I Corps throughout the upcoming fiscal year.
“The major difference between the 4th Infantry Division and the 25th, is that [25th] will continue to preserve some legacy capabilities … and we’re going to make sure that that we maintain seamless integrations with legacy equipment because not everybody’s going to get a fresh fielding like the 4th Infantry Division,” Craven said.
Lockheed’s Marshall said that for its part, the company is making sure the 25th ID gets “back to working operational architecture so that we can continue to build on the capabilities.”
New Environment, Different Technology
Part of the challenge, Army and company officials said, was also just the vastly different environment the tech was called to operate in and on what mobile platforms.
For example, Fort Carson, Colo., where 4th ID is based, is a much more open, plain environment as opposed to the dense jungle in Hawaii with 25th ID. Moreover, 4th ID is a heavier unit, with soldiers operating out of Strykers, while 25th ID’s primary platforms are lighter Infantry Squad Vehicles.
“We don’t have the same type of permissiveness from putting equipment on platforms perspective that we do with like Stryker brigades,” Joseph Welch, the Army’s portfolio acquisition executive for Command and Control (C2) and Counter C2, said in an interview at AUSA. “We’ve had to work through what does that really mean for a mobile infantry unit in terms of what types of transport solutions and what type of compute capacity we can put at echelon. … There’s probably some additional tweaks and optimizations we’re going to make that’s based on just the reality of the formation type.”
As for working with other legacy tech, Cravens said Anduril has been partnering with radio providers, C2IN and 25th ID to on the operational configurations such as how big the channels are, how to separate data from voice channels on radios, how to ensure the appropriate soldiers within a unit have beyond line of sight communications such as Starshield, all in order to provide a “fight tonight” capability for the data layer.
One of the key lessons at Lightning Surge 5, Craven said, was filling the request to go smaller on things like edge computing capabilities. While they integrated Lattice onto the Mounted Family of Computer Systems at 4th ID, last month was the first time they did it on tablets.
However, that integration was requested and done in the middle of the exercise, Craven said, hoping that next time, they’ll have a chance to work that integration before they get out to the field.
Outfitting More Divisions With NGC2
Following the decision to field I Corps with the NGC2 architecture and associated capabilities, the Army is in the process of providing the corps headquarters capabilities and applications while looking to baseline the other divisions.
Taylor echoed the idea that 25th ID is an important first step in that journey given a more representative approach to how the Army will have to field given many of the other formations are closer to them having not received any equipment.
“I think the 25th one was very helpful because those ITN divisions, when we come in with the Next Gen C2 capabilities, that’s the integration that we’re going to do,” he said.
Though, Welch said they’ll continue to upgrade 4th ID with some “burn down items” that came out of Project Convergence over the summer, they need to address in terms of systems to bring forward or leave behind.
Welch noted that the importance of testing over the past year with the ITN equipment in 25th has helped ensure the baseline is solid and they have good configurations.
While there is no definitive timeline in terms of when the other divisions under I Corps will get baselined, Welch said it will occur within the fiscal year. The continuing resolution is having some impact on that, he said, acknowledging they’ll have to look at “pacing” some systems.
Additionally, there are logistics the Army will have to take into consideration in terms of moving systems forward to the divisions, with units spanning up to Alaska and in the Pacific.
Overall, they’re trying to not overwhelm these units with new capabilities.
“We are trying not to have NGC2 coming in there as a disruptor to their mission focus, but as an enabler of it. As you know, NGC2 is a multi-layered stack capability. So our teams are in routine communications for the planning aspect of when we’re going to start introducing those,” he said. “It’s really more aligned to the opportunities that we have when we try to align to their exercises and their training.”

articles.title: Zone 5 ‘found a spot’ in drone interceptor market with new Eclipse: CEO
articles.snippet: CEO Thomas Akers told Breaking Defense that the company’s recent acquisition by Norwegian defense firm Kongsberg offers “an immediate step change” for the startup firm, whose portfolio now spans from a reusable drone interceptor to a low-cost cruise missile.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Defense startup Zone 5 is joining the rush for counter-drone tech, debuting a new interceptor dubbed the “Eclipse” that the company says can combat high-speed, unmanned threats.
Still in development but shown publicly for the first time at the Association of the United States Army conference here, the Eclipse offers a lower-cost, reusable option to take down high-speed drones, Zone 5 CEO Thomas Akers told Breaking Defense.
Arguing that the market is “coalescing” around smaller interceptors that are in turn challenged by more capable drones, Akers said his firm “found a spot” for a larger interceptor with modular payloads.
Larger doesn’t mean too large — an Eclipse model on display at Zone 5’s booth measured 39 in. long and 32 in. wide. But according to Akers, the platform can sport a high-powered microwave that can zap a drone’s electronics, or can carry a kinetic payload to knock one out of the sky. A company fact sheet said the Eclipse can take off and land vertically, achieve speeds of over 200 knots (230 miles per hour) and reach over 30 miles.
Akers said he expects Eclipse to be in development for roughly another six months before entering production, and is initially aimed at the American market. He said the company is aiming to build hundreds of copies a month but declined to comment on an expected price tag, pointing to various potential payloads that influence a final cost.
Akers explained that the Eclipse helps round out Zone 5’s offerings for layered defenses, from a drone-mounted firearm featured on the firm’s Paladin system to its White Spike anti-air missile. Zone 5’s burgeoning portfolio, which includes a cruise missile dubbed Rusty Dagger exported to Ukraine and on order for the Pentagon, likely helped attract the attention of the Norwegian defense firm Kongsberg, which completed an acquisition of Zone 5 earlier this year.
The Kongsberg acquisition “bring[s] kind of an immediate step change” regarding Zone 5’s access to international resources, Akers said. While Zone 5 still operates separately from Kongsberg in the United States, “globally, we present one unified front under the Kongsberg brand.”
The company’s new Norwegian ownership also “gives us access to a larger portfolio of vendors” that can help expand supply chains beyond the US, Akers added. Looking ahead, he said that the firm is going to remain focused on producing low-cost cruise missiles and technologies that can defeat Group 1-4 drones. A key goal is producing thousands of missiles annually, he said, along with leveraging Kongsberg resources to iterate on Zone 5’s products to increase lethality and survivability.
Alongside recent agreements like a Navy program for maritime strike and a Pentagon-wide effort for containerized munitions, one big opportunity for Zone 5, the Air Force’s Family of Affordable Mass Missiles (FAMM) program, is just over the horizon. In the coming years the service plans to acquire tens of thousands of FAMM missiles using multi-year deals, drawing from a pool of vendors including Zone 5, Anduril and CoAspire.
But after using dollars from the One Big Beautiful Bill to kickstart procurement in fiscal 2026, the Air Force once again banked on reconciliation to deliver funds for buying FAMM in FY27 — a prospect dimmed by doubts over another reconciliation bill.
“If multi-year doesn’t happen the way that it’s scheduled to, that sends a clear signal to industry,” Akers said, adding that a shortfall of appropriations means “you’re going to have, definitely, a recoil, and it’s going to be felt beyond just FAMM.”

articles.title: Ahold Delhaize confirms 'malicious actions' behind cyber outages affecting grocery brands
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch multinational grocery retailer, said Monday that a cyberattack forced it to take systems offline across most of its U.S. and European brands, impacting shoppers on both sides of the Atlantic.
articles.full_text:
Ahold Delhaize confirms 'malicious actions' behind cyber outages affecting grocery brands
Ahold Delhaize, the Dutch multinational grocery chain, said Monday that a cyberattack forced it to take systems offline across most of its U.S. and European brands, impacting shoppers on both sides of the Atlantic.
The company confirmed that the suspicious activity it announced detecting in its IT systems last week was caused by malicious actors, adding that it filed a police report in the Netherlands on Monday.
The incident disrupted online services in the U.S., Netherlands and Belgium, although stores remained open. Although the company said it had no evidence that sensitive customer, employee or partner data was stolen, it cautioned that the investigation into the hack remains ongoing.
It did not describe the nature of the attack, nor whether a ransom was involved, stating: “We are not sharing further details that could compromise security measures or interfere with our response efforts.”
The retailer said it was restoring services in phases, and that online shopping services at U.S. brands — including Food Lion and Stop & Shop — are not yet functional, although they are expected to resume in the coming days. The websites and apps for Dutch brands Albert Heijn, Etos and Gall & Gall are back online, though Albert Heijn home deliveries are not expected to resume until Friday.
It said e-commerce services have been restored in Belgium and Central and Southeastern Europe.
Chief Executive Officer Frans Muller apologized for the disruption, saying taking systems offline was a necessary precaution.
“Although this incident was caused by the malicious actions of others, we apologize for the inconvenience this has caused — especially to our customers,” Muller said.
The company said it notified Dutch cybersecurity authorities within 24 hours of detecting the incident.
Ahold Delhaize previously suffered a cyberattack in 2024, causing issues at prominent supermarkets across the U.S. More than 2.2 million people had information stolen from the company’s systems during that incident.

is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: Russian social media giant VK faces disruptions after data center drone strike
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The disruptions began Sunday, when users complained of difficulties loading news feeds, playing music and accessing other features of VK's platforms.
articles.full_text:
Russian social media giant VK faces disruptions after data center drone strike
Thousands of Russian users reported problems accessing the country's largest social network, VKontakte, and its music streaming service over the weekend following a Ukrainian drone strike on a data center near St. Petersburg.
The disruptions began Sunday, when users complained of difficulties loading news feeds, playing music and accessing other features of VK's platforms.
VK confirmed that its facility in the Leningrad region was targeted in the overnight attack on October 18 but denied that the incident had affected its services, saying they remained available as usual. The company did not disclose the extent of the damage or how many servers were affected.
Independent monitoring services, however, recorded a surge in user complaints and a decline in VK's network connectivity. It was not immediately clear whether the disruptions were caused by the strike.
Outage-tracking website Downdetector received approximately 6,600 reports of problems with VK's services on Sunday, including about 600 within a single hour. Another Russian monitoring service, Sboy, registered roughly 2,100 complaints. Internet monitoring organization NetBlocks reported that connectivity associated with VK had fallen to 56% of normal levels during the incident.
By Monday, the number of complaints had declined, according to Russian monitoring service Detector404, although users continued to report problems uploading photos and videos, streaming music, logging into their accounts and sending messages.
Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point said Ukrainian forces used its FP-1 drones to strike several targets in the region, including VK's data center. The company claimed the facility had sustained significant damage, although VK has not confirmed the extent of the destruction.
According to Fire Point, the facility is one of VKontakte's key data centers, responsible for storing and processing user data, including photos, videos and other content. The company cited previously published figures indicating that the site housed more than 20,000 servers in 640 racks.
Ukrainian media outlets and open-source intelligence analysts reported that the strike caused extensive damage to the building, including the partial collapse of its roof. Those reports could not be independently verified.
Pavel Durov, who co-founded VKontakte before leaving Russia and launching Telegram, said Sunday that he had built the data center about 15 years ago, and it was sold to VK a few years later.
"They failed to protect it," he wrote.
VK is one of Russia's largest technology companies, operating the social networks VKontakte and Odnoklassniki, Mail.ru email services and the government-backed Max messaging app, among other products.
The reported outages come amid repeated attacks on data centers in Russia and Ukraine. Earlier in October, Ukrainian forces struck data centers belonging to Russian technology giant Yandex three times. Following the third reported attack, users across Russia experienced problems accessing Yandex services and numerous other websites.
A data center belonging to Sberbank, Russia's majority state-owned banking giant, was also reportedly targeted in a separate attack.
Russia has also repeatedly struck Ukrainian data centers in recent weeks, damaging infrastructure used by businesses and telecommunications providers.
On Monday, Ukrainian telecommunications operator Datagroup said a Russian ballistic missile strike had destroyed equipment and infrastructure at one of its Kyiv data centers, leaving the facility beyond repair.
Russian attacks in September damaged at least six Ukrainian data centers, including facilities operated by MiroHost, Parkovyi, UTELS and Pavutyna.
Moscow has claimed that Ukrainian data centers were being used to support the country's armed forces.

is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Hackers steal customer data from major Russian hosting provider FirstVDS
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Hackers have stolen passwords, access credentials and other sensitive data belonging to customers of Russian hosting provider FirstVDS after exploiting a vulnerability in software used to manage its servers.
articles.full_text:
Hackers steal customer data from major Russian hosting provider FirstVDS
Hackers have stolen passwords, access credentials and other sensitive data belonging to customers of Russian hosting provider FirstVDS after exploiting a vulnerability in software used to manage its servers, the company said over the weekend.
The attack, discovered on Saturday, affected part of FirstVDS's infrastructure, allowing the hackers to access data stored on customers' virtual servers without disrupting their operations.
According to the company, the attackers exploited a vulnerability in VMmanager 6, a virtualization management platform developed by Russian software company ISPsystem. The platform allows hosting providers to manage virtual machines across multiple physical servers.
The hackers then deployed malware that allowed them to copy data from customers' virtual servers, including passwords, cloud service credentials, configuration files, cryptocurrency wallets and other files. The stolen information was transferred to a server controlled by the attackers, according to FirstVDS.
The company said the breach affected only some of its infrastructure but did not disclose how many customers or servers were compromised.
FirstVDS, which has operated since 2002, is one of Russia's oldest hosting providers. It rents virtual private servers that customers use to run websites, applications, databases and other online services. The company also offers servers hosted outside Russia, including in the Netherlands and Kazakhstan.
According to FirstVDS, the attackers were able to access customer data without directly compromising the virtual machines themselves. Instead, the malware mounted their disks in read-only mode, allowing it to copy information without modifying files or disrupting normal operations.
“As a result, there are no traces of the attack on the affected virtual servers, which continue to operate normally,” the company said.
FirstVDS warned customers who received breach notifications to assume that data stored on their servers had been stolen and urged them to change passwords and access credentials.
The company said it had disabled external access to the vulnerable management system and blocked communications with the attackers' server.
ISPsystem has released several patches since the breach, including an update deployed overnight on Monday, but the vulnerability has not yet been fully fixed, according to FirstVDS.
The software vendor has advised against restoring access to the management interface until additional security updates are available.
As of Monday, FirstVDS was still operating with some restrictions, including limited availability of VMmanager functions, according to its service status page.
The company has not disclosed how the attackers initially exploited the vulnerability, which versions of the software were affected or whether the stolen data has been used in further attacks. The identity and motives of the hackers remain unknown.

articles.snippet: Cybersecurity giant Proofpoint says it will acquire Miami-based data visibility and security company Varonis in an all-cash transaction worth $6.3 billion.
articles.full_text:
Proofpoint lines up $6.3 billion deal for Varonis’ data security
Cybersecurity giant Proofpoint says it will acquire a similarly long-running company, Varonis, in an all-cash transaction worth $6.3 billion.
“The combined company will serve more than 16,000 enterprises and millions of organizations globally, creating one of the world’s leading pure-play cybersecurity companies and establishing the industry's largest data and AI cybersecurity organization,” Proofpoint said in announcing the deal on Thursday.
Miami-based Varonis, founded in 2005, focuses on data visibility and security. The footprint for California-headquartered Proofpoint, founded in 2002, traditionally includes email security and identity threat defense. It’s owned by private equity firm Thoma Bravo.
AI figured prominently in Thursday’s announcement. The goal is to create a platform that “helps organizations adopt AI with confidence: finding and protecting sensitive data, controlling what people and AI can access, and stopping data loss.”
Both companies are known for their cybersecurity research.
Varonis researchers recently got headlines for a report in which they manipulated Microsoft’s AI assistant Copilot Personal into explaining how to hack itself.
Proofpoint analysts published research earlier this month about a high-level, apparently China-backed phishing campaign geared toward espionage.
Other big cybersecurity company moves this year include Accenture’s plan to acquire a majority stake in Dragos as part of a broader $4.175 billion deal involving other companies, and Cyera’s $1 billion acquisition of Oasis Security, which closed in September.

articles.title: Moscow police detain suspected DataSuckers hackers linked to breaches in Ukraine and Russia
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Russian authorities have reportedly detained three suspected members of the DataSuckers hacking group following a cyberattack on a popular restaurant chain that exposed vast amounts of customer information.
articles.full_text:
Moscow police detain suspected DataSuckers hackers linked to breaches in Ukraine and Russia
Russian authorities have reportedly detained three suspected members of the DataSuckers hacking group following a cyberattack on a popular restaurant chain that exposed vast amounts of customer information.
A Moscow court on Wednesday placed 19-year-old Denis Fridman under house arrest until December 8 in connection with the Dodo Pizza breach, which reportedly involved the theft of records related to hundreds of millions of orders placed over 15 years. He faces charges connected to the illegal handling of computer information containing personal data.
Fridman is one of four alleged members of DataSuckers, a financially motivated hacking group that has claimed responsibility for recent attacks on major businesses in Russia and Ukraine. Two other suspects have been detained while a fourth remains at large, according to Russian newspaper Kommersant and Telegram news outlet Baza. The suspects reportedly include citizens of Russia, Kazakhstan and Belarus.
According to Baza, police identified the suspected hackers after Fridman accidentally exposed his IP address while accessing data stolen from Dodo Pizza, allowing authorities to trace him to his home in the Russian city of Barnaul.
The attack reportedly began when the hackers discovered Dodo Pizza's corporate credentials exposed on GitHub. Using those credentials, the attackers allegedly gained access to interconnected company systems, including cloud storage and databases, as well as stored passwords.
Kommersant reported that the stolen database was offered for sale on the dark web and that the hackers received $100,000 for the archive, with the money transferred to a shared cryptocurrency wallet. The wallet's password was reportedly changed after Fridman's arrest.
Recorded Future News could not independently verify the circumstances that led Russian law enforcement to the suspects.
Dodo Pizza, a Russian fast-food chain operating approximately 1,500 restaurants across 28 countries, previously acknowledged that attackers may have accessed customer information, including names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth and order details.
Attacks across Russia and Ukraine
DataSuckers has emerged in recent months, claiming responsibility for attacks on major businesses in Russia and Ukraine.
In September, the group claimed responsibility for breaching Russian tour operator Tez Tour, saying it had spent about two weeks inside the company's systems and obtained large amounts of customer information.
The hackers also defaced the company's website. Tez Tour acknowledged the disruption but disputed claims that customer data had been compromised, saying it had isolated its internal systems before the attackers could access them.
Fridman allegedly participated in that attack, according to Kommersant. The newspaper reported that he had previously targeted Ukrainian websites before joining DataSuckers.
Earlier this month, the group claimed responsibility for an attack on ATB, Ukraine's largest grocery store chain, demanding $400,000 and threatening to publish data it claimed to have stolen from millions of customers.
The hackers placed an extortion message and a countdown timer on the retailer's website, which subsequently became unavailable. ATB denied that customer information had been compromised and said it had temporarily taken some online services offline for technical maintenance.
DataSuckers claimed to have obtained records belonging to 7.9 million ATB customers, including names, contact information, addresses and password hashes, as well as employee passport information and more than 11 million order records. Those claims have not been independently verified.
The group describes itself as financially motivated rather than politically aligned. It primarily communicates in Russian and uses a public Telegram channel to announce attacks, publish details of alleged intrusions and invite victims, journalists and law enforcement agencies to contact its members.
In a message posted last weekend, DataSuckers said it was continuing operations but would reduce its public activity.
"We're operating as usual, but you'll be seeing less public activity from us," the group said. "For now, we're focused on specific targets and working on them."
The group has not published any further messages on its Telegram channel since that statement.

articles.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
articles.snippet: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
articles.full_text:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.
In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.
Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.
According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.
Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).
On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.
A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.
That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.
SHINYWIRE
KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.
The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.
The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.
Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).
In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.
The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”
Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.
GHOSTBYTE
According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.
A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.
“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”
It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.
Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).
In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.
“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”
The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.
CONFLICTING INTERESTS
It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.
Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.
In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).
But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.
A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.
The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.
The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.
“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”
In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.
“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.
Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.
That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.
“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”
Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.
“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.
In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.
In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.
The only way to solve this problem is for a federal and state laws to make it illegal to ever pay a ransom. No exceptions.

articles.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
articles.snippet: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.
As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.
The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.
“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”
In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.
TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.
Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.
“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”
As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.
Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.
Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.
Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.
That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.
